summary: The End Junk Fees for Renters Act directs federal regulators to bar application and tenant screening fees on covered rental units, limit late fees to under 3 percent of rent after a 15-day grace period, require pre-lease disclosures of total monthly costs, past litigation, maintenance issues, and 10-year rent history, and have the CFPB and FTC define junk fees while treating their reporting to credit agencies as an unfair debt collection practice.

scores.thoughts: The bill assigns regulatory duties to existing federal agencies (HUD, VA, USDA, FHFA, CFPB, FTC) but creates no new programs, appropriations, or mandates that would expand or contract government outlays. It is purely regulatory.
No provisions address taxes, tax rates, deductions, or revenue measures of any kind.
The bill concerns rental housing fees and disclosures; it has no connection to health insurance, medical care delivery, or healthcare markets.
No provisions relate to firearms, background checks for gun purchases, or gun regulations.
No provisions address immigration status, visas, border enforcement, or pathways to citizenship.
No provisions address reproductive healthcare, abortion access, or related funding restrictions.
No provisions affect military budgets, defense procurement, or veterans' housing programs beyond the incidental regulatory role assigned to the VA for certain mortgage-backed units.
No provisions address environmental regulations, emissions, land use, or climate policy.

While the bill covers some HUD-assisted units that may serve low-income tenants, it does not modify eligibility, benefit levels, or funding for welfare, SNAP, housing vouchers, or similar programs; any effect on tenant costs is incidental and regulatory rather than an expansion or contraction of the safety net itself.
No provisions relate to schools, school funding, choice programs, or federal education policy.
No provisions address drug criminalization, decriminalization, enforcement priorities, or substance regulation.
The bill prohibits fees for criminal-history screening but does not alter sentencing, policing practices, rehabilitation programs, or criminal procedure.
No provisions address tariffs, trade agreements, import/export rules, or globalization.
No provisions affect deficit levels, debt ceiling, or fiscal policy regarding borrowing.
No provisions address nondiscrimination protections, gender identity, sexual orientation, or related civil rights.
No provisions address foreign assistance, international aid programs, or related appropriations.
No provisions address voting access, voter ID, election administration, or campaign finance.

The bill regulates the reporting of unpaid 'junk fees' to consumer reporting agencies and references background checks, but these are narrow consumer-protection measures focused on rental housing rather than broader tech oversight, data privacy standards, or platform regulation.
No provisions address collective bargaining, union rights, wage standards, or employer-employee relations.
No provisions address religious exemptions, civil rights enforcement, or conflicts between religious liberty and antidiscrimination rules.
